utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. If I can just briefly interpose before the next witness; it's just a housekeeping matter and it relates to the next, the following two witnesses, which is Dr. Davor Strinovic and Colonel Ivan Grujic. These are both witnesses that will be testifying in relation to the proof of death of the victims at Ovcara, as well as the widespread and systematic attack against the non-Serb population related to the indictment. And briefly it is an application, Your Honour, in relation to Rule 92 bis (D) which has been previously decided. What the Prosecution would like to do is have the transcripts from both of -- of both witnesses from the Milosevic case to be tendered as evidence and have both witnesses be cross-examined on that particular evidence. Your Honours might recall that the prior, or the expert statements of the witnesses you have indicated that they are likely to be admitted once the witnesses testify here. However, in relation to the transcripts it's not as clear. So it's the Prosecution's position that both the expert statement and the transcript really need to be read together to get the full amount of evidence the Prosecution would like the Trial Chamber to hear. And it may have been a little bit unclear on the applications earlier that prior testimony in the Milosevic case really did dovetail into the expert reports which were submitted. And perhaps it relates more in relation to Mr. Grujic who will be next Monday. Mr. Strinovic will be here tomorrow. And that would be our application.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Have you given notice of this to your Defence colleagues?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I've briefly spoken to Mr. Lukic and Mr. Vasic and unfortunately I didn't get to speak to Mr. Borovic just before the break. And our main concern, especially with Mr. Grujic. And I mean, the reason for the application is to keep the proceedings as short as possible. I think it would probably add an extra day or day and a half's hearing time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: In essence, what you seek is to have both the 92 bis statement and the transcript of prior testimony treated as the evidence in chief of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. There will be some clarification with the witnesses, but in general that would be the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And then both witnesses available fully for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. All I would ask you to is allow us until the next break so that we can consult. Mr. Smith only mentioned this to us a couple of minutes ago, so we would like to have the opportunity to consult. I believe that we will not be putting any objections to that in principle, but we would like to agree on a common position on this matter and then we will be able to state what that is after the following break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. That concludes these matters. We're ready now for the next witness on videolink, and for that purpose we need, pursuant to orders already given, to be in closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The next witness is an expert witness to be called by Mr. Smith. It was anticipated that the cross-examination might take -- and indeed evidence in chief might take a little longer than has done today. Therefore, I am afraid that we are not in a position to immediately commence, but would only be able to start tomorrow morning. We try and ensure that experts are not inconvenienced. And, as I say, we try to estimate as best we can. We had two cross-examinations rather than three today which is, I think, the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's the start of a new and very popular fashion, Mr. Moore. Mr. Borovic is a trend-setter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: That I can believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So can I apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But it's for the right reason, perhaps not the wrong one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: In that --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May I deal with one matter of housekeeping.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It's really simply this: We have now indicated to the Defence the witnesses that we are proposing to call in the next two weeks. As the Court is aware, we have sought witness summons on occasion, and we are not in a position always to know if they are able to give evidence or not, and I wasn't able to do so last week, that's why I performed a -- what I will call forensic minuet in reply in some respects. However, we are able to estimate that the next weeks should be fully occupied. The only thing that I would ask the Court and my learned friends, perhaps, as we come towards the end of the trial, that it may be because of the difficulties for witnesses that they may not be able to come in exactly on the day that we have requested. And consequently, I would ask that my learned friends be prepared for sometimes a change of witness order outside the normal scale. But I would like to think that should not create any significant difficulties for them, and I don't refer to the military witnesses. They're entirely different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I believe it's only right that I should reply and the Defence should probably offer a position. We can understand this situation where certain problems occur with the witnesses. One thing that is important to us, though, is to know which witnesses will be heard over the next two weeks, regardless of the exact chronological order of their appearance. We can always take things in our stride, but the important thing for us is to prepare for all of these witnesses, to know which witnesses will be testifying over the next two weeks, and how much time the OTP are planning on spending with each of these witnesses in terms of their examination-in-chief. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, we stick to our 65 ter estimate. I think 90 per cent of our witnesses have been actually below the estimate. And I would anticipate that that will continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Moore. The Chamber's very clear impression is very different. And we have concluded that your estimates were based entirely on Prosecution evidence and not on the whole of the time for the witness, which is the requirement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, if that's the case, then I apologise. But our estimate, because we can only estimate how long that we will call a witness, we estimate how long it will take for us to call the evidence. We don't know how long cross-examination is going to take.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, you will find the whole estimation process depends on you attempting what you don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, my apologies for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I just reacted there, because we've been significantly misled in estimates.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, it was unintentional misleading to the extent that we believed we were giving estimates of how long our evidence would take.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Not so. Now, the question is the witnesses for the next two weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The witnesses are as we have indicated, and I see no reason to see them change.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, I don't know who they all are. You have mentioned a Mr. Hartman.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I can help the Court. We have got Dr. Strinovic coming tomorrow, or giving evidence tomorrow. That I believe on our estimation of evidence in chief and cross-examination we believe will take probably the rest of the week. For the following week we have got Dr. Grujic. We again estimate that the evidence in toto will take three days. Our estimate is that we should take, I hope, less than a day. And then we have P-030, whom again total estimate is two days. And then for the 6th of June we have P-001 and another witness to follow, and I can't remember if it's a protected witness or not. May I just inquire.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, the second witness appears to be not a protected witness. But in any event that should take, we hope, three days for those two witnesses. And then we start coming into the area of expert witnesses after that. We have Hartman, and Hartman is a witness who is here in The Hague, and we would hope that we would be able to bring that witness in, if there were any gaps, so that we would not waste court time, to use her as a fill-in witness. So as matters stand, we believe that there should be no days lost.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Still concluding around the 16th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's very difficult to estimate. We know how long we'll take in chief. I can only call witnesses. That is all that I can actually do. Our experts, I'm going to try and use what I call the 89(F) technique for both Pringle and Theunens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: There are two other witnesses apart from that, but there is not a significant -- that is the end of it as far as --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ah, there are two witnesses in addition to those you have mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, there are, yes. And Your Honour is aware of a motion in relation to one of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And that would conclude the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There you are, Mr. Vasic. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think all of us here in the courtroom, and especially my learned friend Mr. Moore seem to be in a habit of taking the round about route when talking about witnesses. I have a list based on the 65 ter rule list of the OTP. There appear to be 29 witnesses left on that list, and these are referred to as potential witnesses. The last two times Mr. Moore spoke about this, give us an idea of what to do and what to prepare for over the next two weeks, but I see that Mr. Moore is obviously trying to wrap things up, that he is concluding the OTP's case. It would be nice to have some indication from him which witnesses he has definitely given up on. I know that he is the master of his own case, he decides which witnesses to call, but we still have 25 or 26 witnesses on this list who are potential witnesses and yet Mr. Moore never explicitly refers to them. And this is what I find confusing within the overall framework of our preparations for the next stage, for the final stage, the home straight, as it were, of the OTP's case. The OTP informed us about giving up two particular witnesses about two months ago, but nothing since. We received a motion with some other persons, although this was never made official, that were to be taken off the 65 ter list, and we're still dealing with a relatively large number of witnesses because nothing official has been provided in terms of which witnesses will eventually be left off the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: As I understand it, Mr. Lukic, you've got names now or identifications of seven plus two that have not been specifically identified. Nine to come. Any not among those names, I gather you can take it are not to be called. Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: As a general principle, yes, but not absolutely yes. Because, I'm sorry, so often trying to work out exactly what a Defence cross-examination is going to be, one has to keep so many options available. I'm trying to anticipate what the cross-examination will be. If the cross-examination is as I expect, then I would hope that that will conclude the case. But I'm -- I'm loathe to say I will not be calling such-and-such a witness. That -- those are the witnesses that I believe we will require and that is really all I can say at this stage. We have to rely on what we anticipate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. We will now adjourn until the morning, 9.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 23rd day of May, 2006, at 9.30 a.m. 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 4.35 p.m.,
